subject: Nicolaus Copernicus
overview: Nicolaus Copernicus was a Renaissance astronomer, born in Toruń in Royal Prussia, part of the Kingdom of Poland, who argued that the Earth spins on its axis and travels around the Sun rather than sitting motionless at the center of everything. He spent most of his working life as a church administrator in Warmia, also working as a physician and an adviser on coinage, while he refined his theory in his spare hours. His book On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, printed in the year he died, started the shift in thinking now called the Copernican Revolution.

key_moments.title: Student in Kraków and Italy
key_moments.text: Paid for by his uncle **Lucas Watzenrode**, who later became Prince-Bishop of Warmia, young Nicolaus studied at the **University of Kraków** and then crossed the Alps to Italy. In **Bologna** he lodged with the astronomer **Domenico Maria Novara** and helped him with observations, including watching the Moon pass in front of the star Aldebaran in 1497. He went on to study medicine at **Padua**, and the degree he finally took home, from **Ferrara in 1503**, was a doctorate not in astronomy but in **canon law**.
claims: Nicolaus Copernicus studied at the University of Kraków in the early 1490s.
In Bologna, Nicolaus Copernicus lived with and assisted the astronomer Domenico Maria Novara.
Nicolaus Copernicus observed the occultation of Aldebaran by the Moon in 1497 in Bologna.
Nicolaus Copernicus received a doctorate in canon law from the University of Ferrara in 1503.

key_moments.title: A quiet manuscript moves the Sun
key_moments.text: Before 1514, Copernicus wrote a short sketch of his new system, later known as the **Commentariolus** (Little Commentary), and passed handwritten copies to a few friends. In it he laid out a set of assumptions: the Earth is not the center of the universe, it rotates daily, and it circles the Sun like the other planets. It was never printed in his lifetime, and the copies carried **no author's name** on them.
claims: Nicolaus Copernicus wrote the Commentariolus, a short outline of his heliocentric theory, sometime before 1514.
The Commentariolus circulated in manuscript copies among a small circle of readers.
The Commentariolus was not printed during the lifetime of Nicolaus Copernicus.
The Commentariolus was circulated without the author's name.

key_moments.title: Rheticus arrives at Frombork
key_moments.text: In 1539 a young Lutheran mathematician from Wittenberg, **Georg Joachim Rheticus**, travelled to Frombork in Catholic Warmia to meet the ageing canon. He stayed for about two years, studied the unpublished manuscript, and in 1540 published the **Narratio Prima** (First Account), the first printed description of the Copernican system. Rheticus then took the full manuscript to **Nuremberg** for printing, so the book that put the Sun at the center reached the press through a **Protestant** professor and a Catholic churchman working together.
claims: Georg Joachim Rheticus arrived in Frombork to study with Nicolaus Copernicus in 1539.
Georg Joachim Rheticus published the Narratio Prima in 1540.
The Narratio Prima was the first printed account of the heliocentric theory of Nicolaus Copernicus.
Georg Joachim Rheticus brought the manuscript of De revolutionibus orbium coelestium to Nuremberg for printing.

key_moments.title: De revolutionibus printed
key_moments.text: **De revolutionibus orbium coelestium** came off the press of **Johannes Petreius** in Nuremberg in 1543, dedicated to **Pope Paul III**. When Rheticus left, the printing was overseen by the Lutheran theologian **Andreas Osiander**, who added an unsigned preface saying the theory was only a convenient tool for calculation, not a claim about how the heavens really are. Many readers took that preface for Copernicus's own words until **Johannes Kepler** named Osiander as its author decades later. According to a letter from his friend Tiedemann Giese, Copernicus, by then paralysed by a stroke, was handed a printed copy on the **day he died**, 24 May 1543.
claims: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium was printed by Johannes Petreius in Nuremberg in 1543.
Nicolaus Copernicus dedicated De revolutionibus orbium coelestium to Pope Paul III.
Andreas Osiander added an unsigned preface to De revolutionibus orbium coelestium presenting the theory as a calculating hypothesis.
According to a letter by Tiedemann Giese, Nicolaus Copernicus received a printed copy of De revolutionibus on the day he died, 24 May 1543.

deep_facts.text: The man who rearranged the solar system also worked out one of the basic rules of economics. Asked to help reform the chaotic coinage of Royal Prussia, Copernicus wrote treatises on money in the 1510s and 1520s, observing that when debased coins circulate alongside good ones, people hoard the good coins and spend the bad. The idea is now usually called Gresham's law, after the Elizabethan financier Thomas Gresham, who was not born until several years after Copernicus first put it on paper; economists sometimes call it the Copernicus–Gresham law.
claims: Nicolaus Copernicus wrote treatises on coinage reform for Royal Prussia in the 1510s and 1520s.
Nicolaus Copernicus described the principle that bad money drives good money out of circulation.
The principle that bad money drives out good is commonly named Gresham's law after Thomas Gresham.
Gresham's law is sometimes called the Copernicus–Gresham law.

deep_facts.text: For more than four centuries nobody knew exactly where Copernicus was buried, only that it was somewhere in Frombork Cathedral. Archaeologists dug beneath the cathedral floor in 2005 and found a skull and bones of a man of about seventy. The match came from an unlikely place: a few hairs found pressed between the pages of an astronomical calendar Copernicus had owned, a book carried off to Sweden in the 17th century and kept at Uppsala University. Their DNA matched a tooth and bone from the skeleton, and in 2010 Copernicus was reburied in the cathedral under a new tombstone decorated with a model of his solar system.
claims: The remains of Nicolaus Copernicus were found in excavations at Frombork Cathedral beginning in 2005.
The identification of the remains of Nicolaus Copernicus used DNA from hairs found in a book he had owned, held at Uppsala University.
The book containing the hairs had been taken to Sweden in the 17th century.
Nicolaus Copernicus was reburied in Frombork Cathedral in 2010.

deep_facts.text: De revolutionibus caused little official trouble for seventy years. Only in 1616, during the controversy around Galileo, did the Catholic Church's Congregation of the Index suspend it "until corrected". The corrections it ordered in 1620 were just a handful of sentences, changed so the moving Earth read as a hypothesis, and many surviving copies show owners obediently inking them in, while others ignored them. The book stayed on the Index of Forbidden Books until the 1835 edition dropped it.
claims: In 1616 the Congregation of the Index suspended De revolutionibus orbium coelestium until corrected.
The Congregation of the Index issued its corrections to De revolutionibus orbium coelestium in 1620.
Many surviving copies of De revolutionibus orbium coelestium carry the 1620 corrections written in by hand.
De revolutionibus orbium coelestium was no longer listed in the 1835 edition of the Index Librorum Prohibitorum.

connections.name: Ptolemy
connections.connection: Author of the Earth-centered Almagest system that Copernicus set out to replace, while borrowing much of its mathematics.

connections.name: Johannes Kepler
connections.connection: Defended the Copernican system, replaced its circles with ellipses, and revealed Osiander as the preface's author.

connections.name: Galileo Galilei
connections.connection: Championed Copernican theory with telescope evidence, and the dispute around him led to the 1616 suspension of De revolutionibus.

connections.name: Tycho Brahe
connections.connection: Admired Copernicus's mathematics but proposed his own compromise system in which the Sun circles a fixed Earth.

connections.name: Aristarchus of Samos
connections.connection: Ancient Greek who proposed a Sun-centered cosmos, whom Copernicus mentioned in a passage later cut from his manuscript.
